title: The conference opens and closes at a temple door
body: The first talk (Elder Gong) says temple 54 times; the other twenty-one talks read so far say it 26 times combined, and thirteen of them never say it. The last talk (President Oaks) announces that the Salt Lake Temple opens to the public on April 5, 2027, the first time since 1893. Elder Gong's own talk is a bookend too: it opens and closes on the same joke, 'Why did the temple workers cross the road?'

title: 302 scripture citations; Elder Hathaway's talk is still the crossroads
body: Each speaker leans on a home book: President Oaks's Sunday talk is 15 of 22 Book of Mormon, Bishop Douglas's 13 of 29 Doctrine and Covenants, Elder Renlund's 9 of 16 Old Testament (Israel in the wilderness), and Elder Rasband cites the most of anyone, 40, 22 of them Book of Mormon. Twenty-eight passages are now shared by two talks. Elder Hathaway sits in nine of them, and Elder Matthew J. Eyring, from the afternoon, in eight. Only one passage is in three talks: Alma 7:11–12, the Savior's succor (Elder Hathaway, Elder Soares, Elder Eyring). The closing hymn lists Doctrine and Covenants 76:41–42, inside the 76:39–43 Elder Gong cited in the first talk. And some talks stop one verse apart: Alma 34:32 (Elder Schmeil) and 34:33 (Elder Gong); Helaman 5:11 (Elder Hathaway) beside 5:12, which Elder Runia and Elder Rasband both cite.

title: The Sermon on the Mount, cited in both books
body: Two speakers set the Bible's Sermon on the Mount beside the Savior's sermon at the temple in Bountiful. President Christofferson cites Matthew 5:6 and 3 Nephi 12:6, and quotes the Book of Mormon wording: those who hunger and thirst after righteousness "shall be filled with the Holy Ghost." Bishop Douglas's footnote cites Matthew 5:48 and 3 Nephi 12:48 together, the call to be perfect: "Note the high love of the Savior, along with the high expectations."

title: Jairus's daughter, in Mark and in Luke, twice
body: Elder Hathaway and Elder Kearon, a session apart, both cite the raising of Jairus's daughter in two Gospels, Mark 5:35–42 and Luke 8:49–55. Elder Hathaway takes the Savior's words to the father, "Be not afraid, only believe," and echoes them to everyone still waiting. Elder Kearon takes the lifting, "He lifted the daughter of Jairus from the depths of death," and shows the painting Talitha Cumi, named for the words Jesus spoke to her.

title: Faith is the widest word; love is the loudest
body: Faith (69 mentions) is in 20 of the 22 talks and the closing hymn; only Elder Farnes and Elder Dunn never say it. Love is louder (160) but narrower, 17 talks: Elder Fale says it 34 times, Elder Rasband 29, Elder Gilbert 28. Covenants (102, 17 talks) is carried by two speakers, Elder Morgan (24) and Elder Schmeil (22), while Sister Runia, Elder Sikahema, Bishop Douglas, Elder Dunn and Elder Eyring never use it. The closing hymn carries faith ("my one sure rock of faith") but never says covenant.

title: President Oaks is the voice other speakers build on
body: President Oaks is cited 25 times in 14 of the 20 talks he didn't give. Three talks are built on him: Elder Schmeil on 'Divine Helps for Mortality', Elder Gilbert on five principles from a devotional they gave together, and President Christofferson, whose case against gambling runs on three Oaks lines: 'Where will this lead?', a 1987 moral case, and 'opportunity cost'. In the afternoon he becomes a character: Elder Farnes's main story is Elder Oaks stopping him in a temple dressing room almost 20 years ago ("Brother, tell me how you are really doing") and, years later, not remembering it: "But it's what we do. Isn't it?" Elder Eyring and Elder Rasband both cite his April 2026 talk "Alive in Christ".

title: President Nelson is still cited almost as often as the living prophet
body: President Nelson is cited 19 times across 9 talks, against President Oaks's 25 across 14. Elder Gilbert (5) and Bishop Douglas (4) lean on him most; Bishop Douglas uses President Nelson's youth devotional to make the missionary call, so the call runs from one prophet to the next. President Oaks credits 'the covenant path' to President Nelson by name. In the afternoon Elder Giuffra quotes him on tithing: it "can break cycles of poverty in poor nations and families."

title: Saturday morning runs on Joseph Smith
body: Each of the first six talks quotes or cites the Prophet Joseph Smith. Of the sixteen talks after them, only three cite him, all on Saturday afternoon (Elder Renlund, Elder Chigbundu, Elder Morgan), and Bishop Douglas names him in passing: his closing scripture came "through Joseph Smith" to Thomas B. Marsh. Two of the six go to Liberty Jail: Sister Runia uses the Lord's answer to him there ("all these things shall give thee experience"), Elder Hathaway his cry ("O God, where art thou?"). Elder Morgan cites two lines Joseph Smith wrote there (Doctrine and Covenants 121:1 and 123:17) without naming the jail. Elder Sikahema quotes the First Vision, Elder Caussé and Elder Soares his teachings, Elder Gong his vision of the kingdoms of glory.

title: Saturday carries grief
body: Three of the first five talks hold a death in the family. Sister Runia's oldest son, Ryan, died thirteen years ago; his seven-year-old son gave a Primary talk at the funeral about trusting the designer. Elder Sikahema's grandparents lost their infant son on an ocean voyage to hear an Apostle, then got back on the boat. Elder Hathaway tells of a missionary's father, Kelly, killed in an accident one week before she came home. In the afternoon Elder Eyring adds two more: a friend whose young married son died suddenly and could only say "I can't fix this," and a couple who lost a twin before birth, as he and his wife once did.

title: Christ carries the load
body: Saturday afternoon keeps coming back to one point: Christ carries what we cannot. Elder Dunn's friend Ted quietly carried his pack for the last ten miles of a 100-mile race, and Christ is "an infinitely more amazing load-bearing Friend" who rescues "not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride." Elder Eyring starts from a grieving father's "I can't fix this." Elder Rasband ends on "He's got this!" Elder Dunn and Elder Eyring cite the same verse, Psalm 55:22: "Cast thy burden upon the Lord."

title: For families with someone who has wandered
body: Elder Rasband lists what does not work with a loved one who has strayed: "We preach, cajole, argue, demand, lecture, ignore, sit them down to watch general conference, and even send them links to the talks, like this one." He says he and Sister Rasband have lived it, and asks: "never, never give up on those you love." Elder Morgan is the case from the other side: raised in another church, he finds his conversion came from his ancestors' covenants ("It was covenants"), which do not override a child's agency but leave "a discernible impact" on their posterity. Elder Fale: "you can always come home," pointing to Elder Gilbert's April talk "Come Home".

title: Tithes from Malachi, fasting from Isaiah
body: Elder Giuffra and Elder Soares, a session apart, teach the two offerings: tithing from Malachi's "windows of heaven", the fast from Isaiah 58. They meet in one person. Elder Giuffra's convert in Puerto Montt, Chile, who thought she could never pay, "arrived every week with her tithing envelope and... on the first Sunday of every month she also brought her fast offering."

title: Saturday afternoon teaches with everyday things
body: Cold oatmeal: Elder Renlund's heart-transplant survivor complains, "The oatmeal isn't hot, and the milk isn't cold!", and an asterisk that needs an eraser. The body's immunity (Elder Chigbundu). A glider riding air you cannot see (Elder Kearon). A friend named Ted at mile 90 (Elder Dunn). Baby pictures: "what had you done to earn our love?" (Elder Fale). Elder Rasband even gives the Savior everyday words: "In the vernacular, Jesus Christ says to all who grieve, 'I've got this!'"

title: Eight talks speak as 'I'
body: Eight speakers say 'I' more than 'we': Sister Runia (61 to 56), Elder Caussé (58 to 24), Elder Sikahema (32 to 6), Elder Gilbert (46 to 36), and in the afternoon Elder Farnes (78 to 54), Elder Giuffra (44 to 43), Elder Morgan (64 to 10) and Elder Dunn (56 to 38). Elder Kearon tells the most stories (8), then Sister Runia (7). Elder Gilbert's turning point is a failure of his own: 'I may have won the debate in the moment, but I lost the Spirit.'

title: Love and truth live in one talk
body: Of 36 truth words, 13 are Elder Gilbert's; his title says it: Teach Truth with Love. But love has spread: of 160 love words, Elder Fale has 34 and Elder Rasband 29, ahead of Elder Gilbert's 28. Elder Fale's is a love you cannot lose: "You did not earn it; you cannot lose it." In the morning the runner-up was Elder Caussé (14), who pairs testimony and love as gifts that "echo and strengthen one another". Elder Schmeil, Elder Sikahema, Elder Renlund, Elder Dunn and President Oaks in his closing remarks never say love at all.

title: Faith and secular learning, from two angles
body: President Oaks names two ways of knowing, the scientific and the spiritual, and says there is no ultimate conflict between them. Elder Gilbert tells of staying quiet while academic leaders attacked faith, and a chancellor later asking his help. Doubt and fading faith is the unspoken subject both share.

title: Some talks ask, some promise
body: Across the 22 talks there are 105 invitations and 118 promises. Elder Kearon asks the most (14), then Elder Rasband (10). Elder Soares and Elder Chigbundu promise the most (10 each); three of Elder Soares's answer his one invitation to live the fast in a higher and holier way. Bishop Douglas hangs all four of his promises on one invitation: serve a mission. Elder Sikahema makes no promise at all.

title: The shared picture is a path, and now there is a boat
body: Path pictures show up in 14 of the 22 talks (25 of them): a road, the covenant path, a detour, two paths (giving and taking), the trail to Zion. The closing hymn ends on one more: "the lonely road that leads to thine eternity". Water comes in 7 talks, and the first boat with it: Elder Sikahema's grandparents sail into a storm, bury their son, and get back on the boat.

title: Two phones in one session
body: Elder Sikahema holds up the cell phone as a gift: we can "easily see and hear His anointed servants", and so may take them for granted. Four talks later, President Christofferson holds it up as a danger: "tens of millions of [people] suddenly have casinos in their pockets." Same object, same morning, opposite warnings.

title: Instruments in His hands, echoes of His word
body: Elder Caussé and Elder Soares, three talks apart, make the same promise in the same words: you will "become instruments in His hands". Both also reach for an echo: for Elder Caussé, testimony and love echo each other; for Elder Soares, the latter-day fast is an echo of Isaiah.

title: Concrete announcements, with dates
body: 21 temples to be dedicated this year and 1 rededicated; the Salt Lake Temple open to the public April 5, 2027; a video series, Dedicate, starting right after the session. Bishop Douglas restates that a mission is a duty for young men and "a powerful, but optional, opportunity" for young women. And one forward-looking statement that reads as prophecy: records of Christ's visits to other nations, including the lost tribes, will come forth.

title: The conference ends where it began: a road and a veil
body: Elder Gong opened the conference with temple workers crossing the road "to help the people on the other side", and spoke of hearts softened "on both sides of the veil". The closing hymn's last two verses sing "the light beyond the veil of death" and "the lonely road that leads to thine eternity". Even the scripture listed under the hymn, Doctrine and Covenants 76:41–42, sits inside the passage Elder Gong cited.

title: The last word is a prophet's testimony
body: President Oaks closes his remarks with his witness that truth is found in the restored gospel. Then the congregation sings words written by an earlier prophet, President Gordon B. Hinckley: "I know that my Redeemer lives". The line is Job's (Job 19:25, listed under the hymn), so the conference closes on a testimony that runs from Job through a modern prophet to the people singing it.
